title: Safer housing follows a two-stage ladder in which poverty constrains basic robustness and institutions shape disaster learning
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11319, Why Do Some Countries Build Safer? Economic Constraints, Disaster Learning, and the Two-Stage Housing Quality Ladder
geography: 150 countries/economies, using national housing-robustness measures and disaster, poverty, governance and development indicators

housing_robustness.value: the study constructs national measures of fragile, medium and robust housing from building-taxonomy and vulnerability information

central_signal.value: housing safety is not a single income gradient; the constraints on improvement change across development stages

observations.method: Cross-country analysis using a novel housing-robustness dataset built from Global Earthquake Model building-taxonomy data and linked development, disaster and institutional indicators.
observations.uncertainty: National housing categories aggregate heterogeneous buildings and households; they do not measure actual damage in a specific event or the lived safety of a particular residence.
observations.subgroup: Countries at different development stages, households in fragile housing, earthquake-prone countries, construction sectors, regulators and communities exposed to natural hazards.
observations.counterinterpretation: A national robustness score can improve while vulnerable households remain concentrated in unsafe locations or buildings, and reported associations do not establish a universal policy sequence.

observations.period: First stage of the housing quality ladder; eliminating fragile housing

binding_constraint.value: household poverty is the binding constraint on eliminating fragile housing

poverty_gradient.value: poverty has a strong negative association with housing quality, with non-linear effects that diminish at extreme poverty levels

social_signal.value: basic housing safety is tied to household room and material capacity before higher-order resilience investments can take hold

observations.method: Cross-country regression analysis of housing robustness and poverty measures, with non-linear specifications.
observations.uncertainty: The paper's aggregate associations cannot determine whether income, public housing policy, construction markets, land tenure or other factors produce the observed relationship.
observations.subgroup: Poor households, residents of fragile structures, informal settlements, low-income builders and governments choosing between basic housing upgrades and other urgent needs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Poverty reduction alone may not deliver safer buildings where land, codes, enforcement, materials, finance or hazard exposure remain binding constraints.

learning.value: countries learn from disaster experience, but learning is hazard-specific and mediated by governance quality

institutional_effect.value: earthquake-prone countries benefit particularly from institutional strengthening that enables sustained learning from repeated seismic events

time_dimension.value: resilience accumulates through repeated feedback, institutional memory and implementation rather than a one-time code or rebuilding decision

observations.method: Cross-country analysis relating disaster experience and governance measures to housing robustness, with hazard-specific comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The evidence does not show which institutions or enforcement mechanisms are sufficient in a given country or whether learning reaches informal and low-income construction.
observations.subgroup: Earthquake-prone communities, building regulators, local governments, engineers, builders and residents whose safety depends on code adoption and enforcement.
observations.counterinterpretation: Repeated disasters can also exhaust fiscal and political capacity; observed learning may reflect selective survival or reconstruction rather than durable institutional improvement.

stage_one.value: remove fragile housing under the constraint of poverty and basic material capacity

stage_two.value: once basic fragility is reduced, institutional quality and sustained disaster learning become more important for further improvement

program_implication.value: housing, poverty, infrastructure, governance and disaster policy should be read as one linked social-protection and resilience system

observations.method: Synthesis of the paper's two-stage conceptual framework and cross-country empirical results.
observations.uncertainty: The framework is a comparative research model, not a universal implementation playbook or a causal evaluation of a named housing intervention.
observations.subgroup: Households with different material means, public agencies, housing markets, infrastructure providers and communities facing recurring climate or geological hazards.
observations.counterinterpretation: Countries may move between stages unevenly across regions and tenure types; a national ladder can hide simultaneous basic fragility and advanced engineering in the same place.

related_sources.claim: World Bank reproducibility package documenting the 150-country dataset, Global Earthquake Model inputs, framework and computational verification.
World Bank Tokyo Disaster Risk Management Hub listing the 2026 publication among its resilience and disaster-risk resources.

boundary: This record adds a housing-and-disaster-resilience route linking household material capacity, fragile housing, poverty, building systems, governance, disaster learning and infrastructure safety. It is cross-country aggregate evidence, not a respondent-level survey, event-damage audit, household causal evaluation or proof that reforms reach informal construction.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank working-paper PDF, World Bank reproducibility package and disaster-risk hub listing were reviewed for the 150-country frame, housing-robustness construction, two-stage ladder, poverty constraint, hazard-specific learning and governance qualification.
